did_you_know.text: The biblical phrase “restore your fortunes” does not refer only to returning captives; it can also mean restoring prosperity and well-being.
In the Bible, the “heart” is the center of will, thought, and understanding—not only emotion. “Circumcising the heart” is therefore a metaphor for deep inner change.
The word “niflet” comes from the root פלא, but here it does not mean “wonderful” in the modern sense; it means hidden or beyond reach.
The Sages used the words “It is not in heaven” to teach that the Torah was entrusted to human beings, so Jewish legal decisions do not depend on a new revelation from heaven.
The verse presents the Torah as something people can speak about, understand, and put into practice. It links learning with action.
Calling heaven and earth as witnesses echoes the language of covenants and legal agreements in the ancient world, where witnesses confirmed important commitments.
The verb “to cling” comes from the root דבק, meaning to attach or hold fast. Here it describes loyalty and a close bond, not merely physical contact.
